Oracle Is Cutting Jobs While Spending Billions on AI.
The obvious story is:
“AI is replacing people.”
But Oracle’s numbers point to a more complicated shift.
The company reduced its workforce by around 21,000 employees in the last financial year.
Now, it has started another round of layoffs.
At the same time, Oracle is spending aggressively on AI infrastructure.
Its capital expenditure rose sharply.
It expects to spend roughly $90–95 billion in fiscal 2027.
It is also raising billions through debt and equity to build data centres and expand cloud capacity.
So what is really happening?
Oracle is not simply replacing employees with software.
It is changing what kind of resources its business depends on.
For decades, a software company’s major costs were people:
Engineers.
Sales teams.
Consultants.
Support staff.
Now, the centre of gravity is moving toward:
Data centres.
Chips.
Electricity.
Networking equipment.
Buildings.
Debt.
That changes the economics of the company.
Human labour is relatively flexible.
A company can slow hiring, restructure teams, or reduce headcount.
Data-centre infrastructure is different.
Once Oracle commits to buildings, chips, power contracts and financing obligations, those costs do not disappear easily.
This creates a new business risk:
Oracle may become less dependent on employees—but more dependent on whether future AI demand is large enough to pay for the infrastructure being built today.
That is the real bet.
Oracle has reported strong growth in cloud infrastructure and a large backlog of future contracts.
But growth is not the same as cash generation.
In fiscal 2026, Oracle reported negative free cash flow of approximately $23.7 billion as it continued investing in cloud infrastructure.
This creates a difficult question.
What happens if AI demand grows—but not quickly enough to justify the infrastructure spending?
The company could face pressure from three directions:
Employees face restructuring and job losses.
Investors demand stronger returns on massive capital expenditure.
Lenders expect Oracle to service the debt used to finance the expansion.
This is why the Oracle story is bigger than layoffs.
It may represent a broader transition in the technology industry:
From labour-intensive growth to capital-intensive growth.
The winners may not only be AI model companies.
They may also be the companies supplying:
Chips.
Power.
Data centres.
Cloud capacity.
Cooling systems.
Construction.
Financing.
Meanwhile, software employees may discover that their biggest competitor is not always another engineer.
It may be a company’s rising infrastructure bill.
The question is not whether AI will create economic value.
It probably will.
The more important question is:
Who will capture that value—and who will carry the cost while the industry is still waiting for the returns?

During the past 1 month, Pakistan's technological landscape has received unprecedented attention.

Pakistan's first Google office launched on August 18, followed by Apple's first recent policy level hiring. 

Nevertheless to say, the digital economy sounds at a promising forefront.  

The gains are big. 
The future prospects, bigger. 

Talk bout strategic investment or infrastructure development, Pakistan's technological workforce has it their way. 

However, three weeks later, on 10 September, another important development has received less attanetion:

Articulate announced the biggest change to its platform in a decade.

At Articuland 2026, Articulate announced a major evolution of Articulate 360, including Frontline and the AI-powered Nova.

While very less people might have noticed this change, practically this can have more impact on our jobs than Google's launch.

Here is why the two belong in the same post.

Pakistan's IT export ambition rests on outsourced services, which means these tasks are given out as jobs or contracts. 
 eLearning production is one of the prominent tasks that come under this.

 *Storyboarding, rise builds, storyline development, localisation, voiceover sync* ,  these are some job tasks worth real revenue for real teams in Islamabad, Lahore and Karachi.  

And now Frontline's AI is enabled to take over most of these tasks!

And there is a gap worth watching. 
As of September, there is no published independent evidence that AI-generated training produces better retention.

Somebody has to close that gap. That work has not been automated.

Google's been here now, but has globally been present forever, and this breaks the speed of believing big giants can save the gap. 

On both national and international forums, the question boils down to the same irony:

 If the client can now build the course themselves, what exactly are Instructioanl designers selling?

LEGAL TRANSFORMATION: FROM REACTIVE FUNCTION TO STRATEGIC ENGINE
  
The future of Legal is not simply doing more legal work faster.
  
It is fundamentally changing how the legal function creates value.
  
Many legal departments remain highly reactive.
  
A contract arrives.
  
A dispute emerges.
  
A regulatory issue appears.
  
A business team asks for urgent advice.
  
Legal responds.
  
Then the next issue arrives.
  
This model may keep the department busy—but it does not necessarily make it strategic.
  
Legal transformation requires a different approach.
  
It begins with asking:
  
Why are we doing this manually?
  
Why does the same issue keep recurring?
  
Can we standardise it?
  
Can we automate it?
  
Can we move legal review earlier in the process?
  
Can data help us identify trends?
  
Can the business access appropriate guidance without waiting for Legal every time?
  
Transformation can involve:
  
• Legal technology
 • Contract lifecycle management
 • Standardisation
 • Playbooks
 • Knowledge management
 • Matter management
 • Data and analytics
 • Workflow automation
 • AI-assisted legal processes
 • External counsel optimisation
 • Risk dashboards
 • Legal performance metrics
  
But technology alone does not transform a legal department.
  
Leadership does.
  
The objective should be to redesign the legal function around the needs of the business.
  
Routine work should become more efficient.
  
High-risk matters should receive greater attention.
  
Business teams should receive clearer guidance.
  
Senior lawyers should spend more time on strategic matters.
  
Management should gain better visibility into legal risk and performance.
  
And the legal function should increasingly operate as a source of business intelligence, not merely legal advice.
  
I believe the next generation of legal departments will be distinguished less by the size of their teams and more by their operating models, technology adoption, commercial integration and ability to demonstrate value.
  
Legal transformation is therefore not a technology project.
  
It is a leadership project.

The most dangerous assumption in B2B SaaS? That seat counts will keep growing.

For decades, enterprise software relied on a comforting equation:

More headcount = More seats = More ARR.

But when software evolves from a passive tool into an autonomous worker, headcount stops scaling with output. The pricing model starts working against the product.
Imagine a support team using AI to handle routine tickets. Volume grows, resolution times fall, and customer satisfaction improves.

Then renewal arrives. The CFO asks: If fewer people can handle more work, why are we paying for the same number of seats?

The vendor delivers more value, yet risks a smaller contract. That is the SaaS Pricing Paradox, when you price only on human logins, customer efficiency can become revenue erosion.

Three realities make the transition difficult:

* Outcomes are harder to bill than seats.
Pay per resolved ticket sounds simple. Until the customer reopens it three days later.

Who pays when an AI qualified lead never converts? Without clear definitions, attribution rules, and dispute mechanisms, outcome pricing becomes an argument over what done means.

* Intelligence has a compute floor.
Agentic workflows consume inference, retrieval, and integration resources with every task. Multi step reasoning and repeated retries can make apparently valuable activity unprofitable.

If pricing ignores delivery costs, your busiest customer could become your least profitable one. Usage growth is not automatically margin growth.

* A hybrid model offers a practical path.
A base platform fee can cover governance, security, data management, and administrative access, creating a predictable revenue floor.

Work unit metering can charge for discrete, verifiable work,  a validated claim, a reconciled transaction, or a resolved ticket under agreed rules.

The key is defining the billable unit clearly, pricing for delivery costs, and giving customers visibility into spend. Not every product needs to abandon seats, but seats alone may no longer reflect the value delivered.

Software is no longer just a canvas for human work. It is increasingly doing the work itself.

If your product helps customers grow without hiring, your business model must grow without depending on their headcount. Counting chairs is no longer enough.

How is your board addressing seat-count compression at renewal: defending seats, metering work, or redesigning the model.

We are in a candidate-short market... but sometimes it feels like I’m shouting through bulletproof glass trying to get everyone to hear me. 😂
  
Since March 2026, the NZ tech market has stayed active, but it’s definitely been a more considered, candidate-short cycle. The demand to hire is there, but processes are slower. We’re seeing more steps, more stakeholder alignment and longer decision cycles, even when the need is urgent.
  
I’ve been saying this all year, but we are in a candidate-short market across key skill sets.
  
Why?.. Clients are making more informed decisions around their strategic hires. They’re taking more time to define what they actually need, where the role sits within the wider business and what success looks like. And some candidates are 'passively looking' but they’re often running multiple processes at once. It’s not unusual to see multiple offers on the table.
  
Counter-offers are back. We’re regularly seeing retention moves, title bumps and pay adjustments as employers work to hold onto their best people. Modernisation is still happening. Platform uplift, cloud, security, integration, data and reliability work continues, even when organisations are being more cautious around headcount.
   
Contract roles remain steady. Organisations are still using contractors to keep delivery moving while permanent hiring takes a little longer.
  
Roles we’ve been hiring for/seeing strong demand for across TribeTech:
 (since March)   
🪴 Engineering: Backend, Full Stack, Front End, Mobile and Tech Leads
🪴 Platform / Cloud / DevOps: Platform Engineers, SRE, DevOps, Cloud Engineers and Platform Leadership
🪴 Architecture: Solution, Enterprise, Domain and Platform Architects
🪴 Data: Data Engineering, Analytics Engineering, BI, Data Platforms and Data Consulting, including Fabric and Databricks
🪴 AI / ML: Applied ML, GenAI Engineers, AI enablement and AI leadership, where there’s a clear delivery pathway
🪴 Security: Cloud Security, AppSec and Security Engineering
🪴 Delivery & Change: Delivery Leads, Programme / Project roles, Agile Delivery and Service Delivery Leadership
🪴 Product & Experience: Product Managers, Product Owners, Head of Product, UX/UI, Research and Design Leadership
🪴 Testing & Quality: Automation Engineers, QA Leads and quality uplift roles
  
There’s definitely still movement in the market. It’s just a little less straightforward than it was a few years ago, and both clients and candidates are being more thoughtful about the decisions they’re making.
  
For candidates, that can mean being selective about the opportunities you invest your time in. For employers, it means being clear on what you need, moving when you find the right person, and being realistic about what the market looks like.
  
Anyway…. brain dump complete. 😂
  
Back into sourcing mode!
